name: Bowen's Reaction Series
statement: Silicate minerals crystallize from cooling basaltic magma in a predictable sequence, from high-temperature mafic to low-temperature felsic phases.
statementAccent: from high-temperature mafic to low-temperature felsic phases
meaning: As a basaltic magma cools, different minerals become stable and crystallise out at different, predictable temperatures rather than all at once. Norman Bowen organised this into two parallel branches — a discontinuous series of ferromagnesian minerals and a continuous series of plagioclase feldspar — that together explain why certain minerals are commonly found together in igneous rocks and others rarely are.
mechanism: In the discontinuous series, olivine crystallises first at the highest temperatures and, if it keeps reacting with the melt, converts progressively to pyroxene, amphibole, then biotite as temperature drops. In parallel, plagioclase feldspar crystallises continuously across the range, its composition shifting from calcium-rich (anorthite) at high temperature to sodium-rich (albite) at low temperature. The two branches converge at lower temperatures into orthoclase, muscovite, and finally quartz.

examples.text: Basalts, which crystallise rapidly without much fractionation, commonly contain early-formed olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase, consistent with the high-temperature end of the series.

Granites, representing highly fractionated, slowly cooled melts, are dominated by the low-temperature assemblage of sodium-rich plagioclase, orthoclase, muscovite, and quartz predicted at the bottom of the series.

The Goldich dissolution series shows that minerals crystallising at the highest temperatures (olivine) are the least stable and weather fastest at Earth’s surface, while quartz, formed last, is the most weathering-resistant.

whyItMatters: Bowen’s reaction series explains why particular minerals are typically found together in igneous rocks and provides a framework for magmatic differentiation, by which a single parent magma can produce a wide range of rock compositions. It remains a core teaching and interpretive tool in igneous petrology.
limits: The series was derived largely from experiments on basaltic melts and does not fully describe crystallisation in magmas of very different starting composition. It idealises a continuous cooling history; real magmas are affected by mixing, volatile content, pressure changes, and incomplete reaction that leave zoned or out-of-sequence assemblages.
misreadings: A common misreading treats the series as a rigid, universally followed crystallisation order for all magmas, when it is best understood as an idealised model calibrated to basaltic systems undergoing fractional crystallisation.
origin: Developed by Canadian-American petrologist Norman L. Bowen from laboratory melting and cooling experiments of the early 1900s–1920s, synthesised in his 1928 book "The Evolution of the Igneous Rocks"; often dated to his key experimental papers of the early 1920s.

sources.text: Bowen's reaction series, Wikipedia. — the discontinuous and continuous branches, the mineral order, and Bowen’s experimental method.
"Bowen’s reaction series," Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Bowen’s identity, the crystallisation sequence, and its significance in petrology.
